questions.title: How much memory do 1 billion 768-dimensional float32 vectors take, uncompressed? (TB, where 1 TB is 10¹² bytes.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
10⁹ × 768 × 4 bytes = **3.07 TB**, before the index structure itself. No single machine holds that in RAM, which is why quantisation and sharding stop being optional at this scale.

Three things become mandatory at that scale, not optional optimizations: quantization (IVF+PQ compresses a vector from ~3KB down to roughly 96 bytes — without it, 1B vectors need several terabytes of RAM, which no single machine has), sharding (partition the index across nodes by document type, time range, or an ID hash, fan out at query time, and merge with RRF), and tiered storage (hot, frequently-accessed segments in memory; cold segments on SSD with demand loading). At this scale, fully managed services get prohibitively expensive, and self-hosted Milvus or FAISS across a node fleet becomes the standard choice; budget 48–72 hours for a full from-scratch index build, with incremental indexing for ongoing updates.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Your index will hold 1.5 billion vectors. You have one node with 64 GB of RAM and a fast SSD, and 5 ms latency is acceptable. HNSW or DiskANN?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Once the corpus is large enough that an in-memory HNSW graph becomes RAM-prohibitive — roughly past 100–200M vectors, and certainly in the 1B+ range, where HNSW's full-precision, fully-resident graph would need several terabytes of RAM. DiskANN keeps only PQ-compressed vectors in RAM for graph navigation and stores full-precision vectors on SSD, fetched only to re-rank a small final candidate set — published numbers show ~95% recall at low-single-digit-millisecond latency over a billion points on a single node with just tens of gigabytes of RAM. The cost is a small amount of added per-query latency from the SSD reads, which is fine for most RAG workloads but not for a sub-millisecond latency requirement.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: HNSW.
options.why: HNSW keeps the full graph and vectors in RAM: terabytes at this scale.

options.text: DiskANN.
options.why: Compressed vectors in RAM guide the search, and full vectors on SSD re-rank the final candidates.

options.text: BM25.
options.why: A different kind of retrieval that doesn't replace a vector index.

options.text: Brute-force scan.
options.why: Far too slow over 1.5 billion vectors.

questions.title: What's the cold-start problem in vector database deployment, and how do you mitigate it?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: After a restart or a new node joining, the index graph has to be loaded from disk into RAM before it can serve fast approximate search — until that finishes, queries either fall back to slow linear scan or fail outright. Mitigations: pre-warm with a batch of probe queries right after load, before accepting real traffic; never restart the primary node directly, scale via warm read replicas instead; memory-lock the index (`mlock`) so the OS can't page it out under memory pressure; and use memory-mapped index files so segments can be paged in lazily rather than requiring a full blocking deserialization at startup.

questions.title: Serverless vs. provisioned vector database — what's the actual tradeoff, not just the marketing pitch?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Serverless (Pinecone Serverless, Zilliz Cloud Serverless) bills per operation and per-GB stored, so idle time costs almost nothing — ideal for bursty or intermittent traffic — but the first query to a cold namespace after inactivity can take hundreds of milliseconds to a couple of seconds while it loads into a shared worker, and that latency is architectural, not something you can tune away. Provisioned/dedicated deployments charge a fixed cost per node-hour regardless of utilization but stay warm with consistent low latency and no cold-start penalty. At high, steady query volume, provisioned is usually cheaper and more predictable; at low or spiky volume, serverless avoids paying for idle capacity you don't use.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: Given the choice, should you fine-tune the reranker or the embedding model first?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The reranker, in nearly every case. It needs less labeled data (pairwise cross-encoder training is more data-efficient than bi-encoder contrastive training), and critically, it requires no re-indexing when it changes — it only rescores an already-retrieved candidate set, so you can iterate on it daily. An embedding fine-tune forces a full corpus re-embed before you can even evaluate the change in production, which is a far more expensive and slower feedback loop.

options.text: Both at once.
options.why: Then you can't tell which change helped.

options.text: Neither. Prompt changes are enough.
options.why: Prompts can't fix a retriever that ranks the wrong documents.

options.text: The reranker: it needs less data, and changing it doesn't require re-indexing.
options.why: You can try a new reranker the same day. A new embedding model needs the whole corpus re-embedded first.

options.text: The embedding model, because retrieval comes first.
options.why: Its improvements can't even be measured until the whole corpus is re-embedded.

questions.title: Why do hard negatives matter more than random negatives when fine-tuning an embedding model with contrastive loss?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Random negatives are usually trivially irrelevant to the query, so the model learns almost nothing from them — it already knew they didn't match. Hard negatives, mined via BM25 or the model's own current encodings, are lexically or semantically close to the query without actually being relevant, which is exactly the decision boundary the model actually needs to learn to improve. The catch is hard-negative mining can surface genuine false negatives — documents that are actually relevant but just weren't labeled as such — which poison training unless filtered out, typically by dropping any "negative" a cross-encoder scores suspiciously high.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

options.text: Hard negatives are cheaper to collect.
options.why: They're more expensive: you have to mine them.

options.text: Random negatives cause overfitting.
options.why: They mostly cause slow, shallow learning.

options.text: Hard negatives never include mislabelled positives.
options.why: They often do. Mined "negatives" that are actually relevant have to be filtered out.

options.text: Random negatives are almost always obviously irrelevant, so the loss on them is near zero and teaches little.
options.why: Hard negatives sit on the boundary the model actually gets wrong.

questions.title: What operationally happens after you deploy a newly fine-tuned embedding model into production?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Every vector in the entire corpus has to be regenerated, because old and new embeddings live in geometrically incompatible spaces — you cannot mix vectors from two model versions in one index without silently corrupting every similarity comparison involving one old and one new vector. In practice that means budgeting real compute and hours-to-days of pipeline time to re-embed the full corpus, building the new index alongside the old one and cutting over atomically (blue/green) rather than updating in place, and having a plan for documents that arrive during the migration window so they don't accidentally get embedded with the wrong model version.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is catastrophic forgetting in the context of domain fine-tuning an embedding model, and how do you detect it?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It's when gradient updates optimized entirely for domain data overwrite general-purpose semantic representations the model learned during pretraining — the model gets measurably better on your domain but quietly worse at everything else. Detect it by holding out a general-domain eval slice (a BEIR subset, for example) alongside your domain eval set, and reporting recall/MRR/NDCG on both before and after fine-tuning; a healthy fine-tune shows a large domain gain with only minor general-slice drift, while a sharp general-slice drop signals forgetting rather than genuine adaptation.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What distinguishes Advanced RAG from Naive RAG, concretely?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Advanced RAG is Naive RAG plus a defined set of pre- and post-retrieval enhancements applied as a fixed pipeline: query rewriting/HyDE before search, hybrid dense+sparse retrieval instead of dense alone, and a reranking pass before generation. It's still a single fixed pass end to end — the thing that distinguishes it from Modular RAG isn't the techniques themselves, it's that Advanced RAG bakes them into one unchangeable sequence rather than exposing them as swappable, routable components.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Modular RAG, and what's the one thing that actually separates it from Advanced RAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Modular RAG restructures the pipeline into independently swappable components — a router that picks which retrieval strategy or data source to use per query, pluggable retrievers, a fusion module, memory — rather than one fixed sequence. The single distinguishing mechanism is the *routing/orchestration layer*: Advanced RAG always runs the same steps in the same order; Modular RAG decides, per query, which modules to invoke at all.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Speculative RAG, and when does its drafter/verifier split actually pay off?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A small, fast "drafter" model partitions retrieved documents into subsets and generates a candidate answer plus rationale from each subset in parallel; a larger "verifier" model then reads all the drafts and rationales (not the raw documents) and picks the best one — borrowing the same draft-then-verify shape as speculative decoding, but applied to RAG's retrieve-then-generate step instead of token generation. It pays off when you have enough traffic to amortize running two models and your corpus naturally partitions into genuinely distinguishable subsets; it doesn't help a low-traffic system, and it degrades if the subsets are too similar for the drafts to meaningfully disagree.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Long-context RAG, and when should you reach for it instead of standard chunked retrieval?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Instead of retrieving a small set of precise chunks, it stuffs a much larger span of raw document(s) — sometimes a coarse-selected document is fed in nearly whole — directly into a long-context model's window, trading retrieval precision for not having to get chunk boundaries exactly right. It's worth it when your corpus is small enough to plausibly fit (hundreds of documents, not hundreds of thousands), when precise chunk-boundary retrieval keeps failing on your content, or when prompt caching on a stable document set makes the token cost of repeated long-context calls cheap; it breaks down once the corpus genuinely exceeds what any context window — even a large one — can hold.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How does RAFT (Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning) differ from standard supervised fine-tuning on QA pairs?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: RAFT trains explicitly on retrieval's actual failure distribution: each training example includes the real golden document plus several distractor documents a retriever would plausibly surface, and critically, some fraction of examples omit the golden document entirely so the model also learns when *not* to trust the "retrieved" context and fall back to its own reasoning. Standard fine-tuning on clean QA pairs never exposes the model to distractors or to retrieval-miss scenarios at all, so it doesn't learn the specific skill RAFT targets: staying robust when retrieval is imperfect, which it always eventually is in production.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is RAG-Fusion, and how is it different from plain multi-query retrieval?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Both generate several rephrasings of the query and retrieve for each — the difference is in how the results combine. Multi-query retrieval takes a simple union of the result sets; RAG-Fusion instead merges the *ranked lists* via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well across several of the rephrasings is rewarded for that consistency rather than just being counted once like everything else in the union.

questions.title: Each hop in a 4-hop retrieval chain is 90% reliable, independently. Roughly how reliable is the whole chain? (As a decimal.)
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
0.9⁴ = **0.656**. Four individually good hops give a chain that's right only about two thirds of the time, because each hop builds on the last one's answer.

It retrieves and reasons across several sequential hops — each hop's query is informed by what the previous hop found — to answer questions that need facts chained across documents a single retrieval pass would never connect. The central new risk is error accumulation: if an early hop retrieves a plausible-but-wrong intermediate fact, every subsequent hop inherits and compounds that error, so a chain of individually-90%-reliable hops can end up substantially less reliable end-to-end than any single hop in isolation.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is HippoRAG, and why does it use Personalized PageRank instead of simple graph traversal (BFS/DFS)?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It builds a knowledge-graph-like index (inspired loosely by how the hippocampus indexes associative memory) and, at query time, seeds Personalized PageRank on the entities mentioned in the query to find the most relevant connected subgraph. PageRank over simple BFS/DFS because it naturally handles *multiple, weighted paths* to a candidate answer — a node reachable by several independent, meaningful routes accumulates more relevance score than one reachable by a single long accidental path, which a pure breadth/depth traversal has no way to express.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is KAG (Knowledge-Augmented Generation), and what gap does it target that plain GraphRAG doesn't?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: KAG adds "mutual indexing" (keeping the knowledge graph and the source text tightly linked so reasoning can fall back to raw text when the graph is incomplete) and logical-form-guided reasoning, where parts of a query are answered by deterministic logical operations over the graph rather than leaving everything to free-form LLM generation. The gap it targets is graph incompleteness and reasoning reliability: plain GraphRAG's community-summarization approach has no mechanism for formally verifiable multi-step reasoning, and nothing to fall back on when the graph itself simply doesn't contain a needed fact.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What do GraphReader and GNN-RAG have in common, and how do they differ from each other?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Both use a graph structure for multi-hop reasoning but push the exploration work onto something other than an LLM manually traversing edges. GraphReader has an agent explore the graph step by step and carry forward only compressed findings (so the full document never has to sit in context at once); GNN-RAG instead trains an actual graph neural network to do the retrieval/traversal itself and hands its output to the LLM only for final verbalization — a learned retrieval mechanism rather than an agentic exploration loop.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is REALM, and what made it historically significant even though almost nobody deploys it unmodified today?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: REALM trains its retriever *end-to-end*, jointly with the language model, through a latent-variable objective — the retriever learns directly from downstream task loss which documents are actually useful, rather than being frozen or trained separately. It's significant as the architecture that first proved joint retriever training was possible at all, but its asynchronous-index-refresh problem (the retriever's embeddings and the serving index drift apart during training) was awkward enough that most RAG research since moved toward frozen-retriever, prompted-generator designs instead.

questions.title: What is RETRO, and how does chunked cross-attention let it scale to a trillion-token datastore?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: RETRO retrieves nearest-neighbor chunks from a (frozen, unlearned) massive datastore and injects them into generation via chunked cross-attention — each output chunk attends to the retrieved neighbors of the *input* chunk immediately preceding it, rather than concatenating retrieved text into the prompt. Because the retriever is frozen (no joint training) and the datastore lookup is a cheap nearest-neighbor search rather than something requiring gradient updates, RETRO can scale its external datastore to sizes (trillions of tokens) that would be completely infeasible to encode into model weights.

questions.title: What is Atlas, and why is retrieval especially valuable in the few-shot setting specifically?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Atlas jointly trains a retriever and a reader (Fusion-in-Decoder-style) and is evaluated specifically on how well it performs with very few labeled training examples. Retrieval is unusually powerful in the few-shot regime because it supplies the factual knowledge a model would otherwise need many labeled examples to memorize — with retrieval doing that work, the few available labeled examples can be spent entirely on teaching the model the *task* (how to read and answer), not on teaching it facts it can instead look up.

questions.title: What is Fusion-in-Decoder, and why does it scale better than just concatenating all retrieved passages into one input?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Each retrieved passage is encoded *independently* by the encoder (cheap, and parallelizable), and only the decoder attends jointly across all of their encoded representations when generating the answer — evidence from different passages can only interact inside the decoder, never earlier. This scales far better than concatenation because the expensive quadratic self-attention cost of the encoder is paid per-passage rather than across the full concatenated length of all passages at once, letting FiD fuse far more passages than a single-encoder-over-everything approach could afford.

questions.title: What is Tree-of-Thought RAG, and what does it add over a single ReAct-style retrieval loop?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It explores multiple reasoning branches in parallel, each potentially triggering its own conditional retrieval, and prunes weaker branches rather than committing to one linear think-retrieve-think chain the way ReAct does. It's worth the extra cost specifically for questions where the right reasoning path genuinely isn't obvious upfront and backtracking would otherwise mean restarting the whole chain — not for straightforward lookups where a linear loop was already going to work.

questions.title: What is DPR (Dense Passage Retrieval), and what's its one foundational contribution to everything that followed?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: DPR is the paper that established the now-default dense retrieval architecture: a bi-encoder, trained with contrastive loss to pull relevant query-passage pairs together in embedding space, compared by inner product (or cosine similarity) instead of hand-designed term-frequency heuristics like BM25. Its lasting contribution is proving that *learned* dense representations could outperform classical sparse retrieval on open-domain QA at all — essentially every dense-retrieval architecture discussed elsewhere on this page descends from this result.

questions.title: What is WebGPT, and how is it different from simply prompting a model to use a search tool?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: WebGPT's model weights themselves — not a prompt — encode when to search, click, and quote, learned via RLHF by training a reward model on human preferences between pairs of full browsing transcripts. Prompted tool use relies on an already-capable general model's in-context reasoning about when to call a tool; WebGPT instead fine-tunes the policy itself specifically for the browsing task, which was a meaningfully different (and at the time, novel) approach before general-purpose models got good enough at prompted tool use to make this specific route less common.

questions.title: What is SURGE, and what specific failure does programmatic schema enforcement fix that “just ask the model for JSON” doesn't?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A standard RAG system asked to output structured JSON can produce a structurally valid response with semantically hallucinated field values — it has no mechanism distinguishing "I found this in the retrieved passage" from "I'm generating a plausible-sounding value." SURGE fixes this with a per-field gate: schema enforcement validated at the API/tool-call layer (not just requested in a prompt) combined with an NLI model that checks whether the cited passage actually entails each specific claimed field value, rather than just checking the output parses as valid JSON.

questions.title: What is Recursive Document Summarization RAG, and how is it different from RAPTOR?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Both build a hierarchical tree of summaries, but the tree boundaries differ fundamentally: Recursive Document Summarization builds top-down *within* each source document (every node belongs to exactly one document, preserving provenance), while RAPTOR clusters chunks *across* document boundaries bottom-up by semantic similarity, so a single RAPTOR summary node can blend content from several unrelated source documents. Choose document-level recursive summarization when provenance matters (citing exactly which document a summary came from); choose RAPTOR when cross-document thematic clustering is the actual goal.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Search-R1, and how does it differ from prompted Agentic RAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Search-R1 trains the retrieve-or-reason decision itself via reinforcement learning against task reward, rather than relying on a frozen model's prompted judgment about when to search. It's the RL-trained analogue of what Agentic RAG does with prompting — same behavioral shape (deciding whether/when to search mid-reasoning), but the policy is learned from outcome reward instead of being a frozen model following in-context instructions.

questions.title: What is Deep Research (as an architecture), and what's the one thing that actually distinguishes it from an agentic loop with a higher step limit?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The distinctive mechanism is *upfront decomposition into independently parallelizable sub-questions* — not simply running more search rounds in a loop. A single agentic loop with a higher iteration cap still processes searches sequentially within one growing shared context (hitting the same "lost in the middle" risk that long accumulated context always has); Deep Research instead splits the research brief into sub-questions narrow enough for dedicated sub-agents to research independently and in parallel, each in its own isolated context, merging findings only at the end.

questions.title: What is MemoRAG, and how does it differ from RAPTOR?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: MemoRAG generates a corpus-aware "draft" or clue *before* retrieval, from a model that has actually compressed the entire corpus — effectively asking "given everything this corpus contains, what would evidence supporting an answer to this query actually look like," rather than relying on the raw query's vocabulary alone to drive embedding similarity. RAPTOR, by contrast, builds its hierarchy once at index time and doesn't generate anything new per-query; MemoRAG's distinctive step happens at query time, informed by global corpus understanding the raw query alone wouldn't carry.

questions.title: What is LongRAG, and how is it different from Long-context RAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: LongRAG rebalances retrieval-unit *size*, not retrieval timing — it groups text into units roughly 30x larger than typical RAG chunks, deliberately making the retrieval problem easier (fewer, more distinguishable units to search among) at the cost of making the reading problem harder (the reader has to find and synthesize the answer within a much longer, less-targeted span). Long-context RAG is about stuffing a large span of raw text into the model at generation time; LongRAG is specifically about what size the *retrieval units themselves* should be.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is VisRAG, and what's the one thing that separates it from every other architecture discussed here?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: VisRAG treats the rendered page *image* as the sole unit of both retrieval and generation, with no text-extraction step anywhere in the pipeline — every other architecture, including standard Multimodal RAG and Table-Aware RAG, still extracts and normalizes content into text (or a text-adjacent structured form) at some point before embedding or generation. VisRAG instead bets entirely on a vision-language model's ability to perceive text, tables, figures, and layout jointly from raw pixels, for both deciding relevance and producing the final answer.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is LazyGraphRAG, and why does it index for close to the cost of plain vector RAG when GraphRAG and LightRAG don't?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It defers all LLM-based summarization from index time to query time — instead of GraphRAG's "summarize every community whether or not it's ever queried," it only summarizes the specific subgraph a given query's relevance-testing loop actually surfaces. The index itself is built with zero LLM calls (just cheap, deterministic noun-phrase extraction and co-occurrence counting), which is exactly what keeps indexing cost comparable to plain vector RAG rather than paying GraphRAG's and LightRAG's substantial upfront LLM-extraction-and-clustering bill.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Astute RAG, and what does it do differently with the model's own prior knowledge?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It treats "what the model already knows" as an explicit, tagged, competing information source rather than an implicit fallback the model quietly leans on. Standard RAG conditions generation on retrieved passages and hopes the model's own judgment sensibly fills any gaps; Astute RAG instead deliberately elicits the model's internal knowledge, tags it exactly like an external retrieved passage, and runs both through the same explicit consolidation/conflict-resolution step — rather than one silently overriding the other with no visibility into which actually won.

questions.title: What do Auto-RAG and DeepRAG have in common, and how do they differ from CoRAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Both make the retrieve-or-reason choice a first-class decision at *every* reasoning step — a step can resolve entirely from parametric memory with no retrieval call at all. CoRAG, by contrast, chains a sequence of retrieval steps where retrieval happens at every step of the chain by construction; its tunable dimension is chain *length* and what to retrieve at each hop, not whether to retrieve at all — a distinction that matters because Auto-RAG/DeepRAG can be meaningfully cheaper on queries that don't actually need external knowledge at every step.

questions.title: What is CoRAG, and what does it mean that chain length is “an explicit, trained-in test-time compute knob”?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: CoRAG fine-tunes a model specifically on retrieval-reasoning chains proven correct via rejection sampling, so the query-reformulation skill itself is optimized against outcome correctness rather than whatever a frozen model happens to produce when prompted to "think step by step and search." Because chain length is something the training process explicitly learned to vary, it becomes a tunable lever at inference time — you can trade more hops (more compute, better odds on hard questions) for fewer (cheaper, fine for easy ones) as a deliberate dial, not just an emergent side effect of prompting.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is RQ-RAG, and how is it different from always applying one fixed query-rewriting technique like HyDE or Step-Back?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: RQ-RAG is a fine-tuned, per-query action-selection policy expressed via special control tokens — rather than applying one hand-chosen transformation uniformly to every query, the model decides, per query, which of several operations (rewrite, decompose, disambiguate, or none) actually fits. A compound question gets decomposed, an ambiguous one gets disambiguated, an already-fine query passes through untouched — this per-query adaptivity is exactly what a single fixed prompted strategy applied to every query can't do.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is REFRAG, and what third option does it introduce beyond “include a chunk fully” or “don't retrieve it”?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: REFRAG compresses every retrieved chunk to a single dense embedding by default, with a lightweight RL-trained policy selectively "expanding" only the chunks it judges important back into full raw tokens for that specific query. Standard RAG only has two states per chunk — fully included, or not retrieved at all — while REFRAG adds a third: "included, but compressed, with the option to zoom in," which is what lets it extend effective usable context roughly 16x at a comparable latency budget, instead of forcing a flat tradeoff between context breadth and decoding speed.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Few-Shot Example RAG, and how does it differ from standard document RAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Instead of retrieving documents to ground a factual answer, it retrieves similar *past examples* (demonstrations) to populate a dynamic few-shot prompt for in-context learning — common in text-to-SQL and other structured-generation tasks where "show it a similar solved case" beats a static hand-picked few-shot set. The retrieval target is categorically different: not "facts relevant to this question" but "prior demonstrations whose pattern this new case should follow."
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is Agentic Web RAG, and how does it differ from corpus-based RAG beyond “it searches the internet”?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It replaces a fixed, pre-indexed corpus with live web search and page fetching as the retrieval mechanism, which introduces problems corpus-based RAG doesn't have at all: source quality and reliability vary per result and have to be actively assessed, citation tracking has to be a first-class architectural component (not an afterthought) since users need to verify claims against live, changing sources, and the fetch layer itself is a real security surface — an attacker-controlled page can attempt prompt injection or redirect the fetcher to internal/unintended endpoints, which a closed, pre-vetted corpus simply can't do.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: A RAG answer has a citation next to every sentence. Which check tells you the claims are actually supported?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A citation just means the model pointed at *some* passage near the claim — it doesn't guarantee that specific passage actually entails the specific claim being made next to it. Real verifiability requires checking at the claim level: citation precision (of the passages cited, how many genuinely support the claim), citation recall (of the claims made, how many have any supporting citation at all), and attribution accuracy (does the cited passage actually say what the response claims it says, checked via NLI entailment) — three genuinely separate failure modes a model can hit independently even while technically "citing sources."

questions.title: What is Privacy-Preserving RAG, and what are the main technical levers for keeping a corpus's content from leaking through the system?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Techniques span the whole pipeline: on-device or federated embedding so raw sensitive text never leaves a trust boundary, differential privacy noise added to retrieval signals or training data, and strict output filtering/redaction for PII before a response is returned. The hard part in an interview answer isn't naming the techniques, it's being honest that most of them trade real quality or latency for privacy guarantees — there's no free version of this, and the right combination depends entirely on the actual threat model (internal misuse vs. external breach vs. regulatory compliance).

questions.title: Why does standard RAG underperform specifically on tables, and what does Table-Aware RAG do differently?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Standard RAG treats a table as just another block of prose and chunks it by character count, which destroys the row/column structure that gives a table its meaning — a chunk boundary can split a row from its header, or merge unrelated rows together with no indication of which value belongs to which column. Table-Aware RAG's distinctive mechanism is structure-preserving linearization: explicitly parsing rows, columns, and headers into a structured representation first, then converting that structure back into text designed for retrieval and arithmetic reasoning — either full-table Markdown, or per-row chunks with the header re-attached to every single row so each chunk stays self-contained.

options.text: LLMs can't read tables.
options.why: They read well-formatted tables fine. The trouble is the mangled chunks they're given.

options.text: Embeddings can't represent numbers.
options.why: They represent them poorly, but the bigger problem is losing which value belongs to which column.

options.text: Fixed-size chunking breaks rows and columns apart, separating values from their headers. Parse the table and keep the header with every row.
options.why: Each chunk then makes sense on its own.

options.text: Tables are too short to be retrieved.
options.why: Length isn't the issue. Structure is.

questions.title: What is Streaming/Real-Time RAG, and what's the core mechanism that separates it from standard batch-indexed RAG?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: The distinctive mechanism is continuous, incremental index updates as new data arrives, rather than periodic batch re-indexing — new documents (or events) become searchable within seconds to minutes instead of waiting for the next scheduled rebuild. This matters for use cases like live news, fast-moving incident response, or trading desks, where a correct answer five minutes ago can be actively wrong right now, and a standard nightly-rebuild RAG pipeline's staleness window is itself the failure mode.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: What is LightRAG, and how does its dual-level retrieval differ from Microsoft GraphRAG's community-hierarchy approach?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: LightRAG indexes at two levels simultaneously — fine-grained entity-level relationships for specific queries, and higher-level thematic summaries for broad ones — and lets a query mode choose which level (or both) to search, without needing GraphRAG's expensive community-detection clustering step at index time. The practical consequence is a meaningfully cheaper, faster index build, at the cost of GraphRAG's more thorough corpus-wide thematic coverage from pre-computed community summaries.
questions.followup: What assumptions does your answer depend on, and when would you choose a different approach?

questions.title: How do you prevent an agentic RAG loop from running forever (or effectively forever, on your bill)?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Combine four stopping conditions rather than relying on just one: a hard iteration cap as the absolute last resort (e.g. max 6 loops); a semantic-drift check that flags when the agent starts issuing near-duplicate retrieval queries (high cosine similarity to a prior query in the same loop signals it's spinning); a cheap sufficiency check, where a small model reads the accumulated context and outputs a simple yes/no on whether it's enough to answer; and a token/cost budget guard that stops before the context window or a spend limit is hit. In practice the sufficiency check fires most often in healthy operation — the hard cap and budget guard are safety nets for genuine edge cases, not the primary mechanism.

options.text: Several stopping rules together: a sufficiency check, a near-duplicate-query check, a token budget, and a hard iteration cap.
options.why: The cap and budget are safety nets. The sufficiency check does most of the stopping.

options.text: Tell the model to stop when it's done.
options.why: Unreliable on its own. Looping models rarely notice they're looping.

options.text: A wall-clock timeout only.
options.why: It ends runaway loops, but only after paying for them.

options.text: A hard cap of 50 iterations.
options.why: A cap alone stops runaways late and expensively, and does nothing for an agent that's spinning.

questions.title: ReAct vs. Plan-and-Execute for agentic RAG — when do you reach for each?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: ReAct interleaves reasoning and retrieval in a serial loop, where each observation informs the next step — highly adaptive, since it can change approach mid-loop, but every hop adds latency because steps can't run in parallel. Plan-and-Execute separates planning from execution: one call produces a full task list up front, then everything in it runs in parallel — faster when the task decomposes predictably, but brittle, since there's no replanning if the upfront plan turns out to be wrong partway through. Use ReAct when the query's scope is genuinely unknown and you need adaptive exploration; use Plan-and-Execute when the decomposition is predictable and latency matters more than adaptivity.

questions.title: What does a Reflection/Correction agent actually catch that a single-pass RAG system misses?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It re-reads the retrieved chunk it just cited alongside the model's own draft answer and checks whether the chunk *actually* supports the specific claim being made — not just whether some chunk was retrieved at all, but whether this particular sentence is traceable to this particular chunk's text. A single-pass system has no mechanism to catch the case where a plausible-sounding number or fact simply wasn't in the retrieved context at all; a reflection agent flags that case and can trigger a more targeted re-retrieval before the draft ever reaches the user.

questions.title: How do you make an agentic RAG system observable in production, given that failures can be two or three hops removed from the wrong final answer?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Instrument three things specifically: per-iteration traces (log each step's query, which tool was called, a summary of the result, and tokens used, with an iteration index, so you can replay the whole chain); the *terminal reason* the loop stopped (reached a real answer, hit the iteration cap, tripped the drift check, or exhausted budget — distinguishing "answered correctly" from "gave up" is not optional for debugging); and user-visible citations tracing which retrieved passages actually contributed to the final answer. Without per-iteration traces specifically, debugging a multi-hop agent is close to impossible, because the root cause is routinely several steps upstream of where the wrong answer actually surfaces.

questions.title: How do you decide which agent framework to use for a given agentic RAG project?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Match the framework to what's actually hard about the use case, not to popularity — LlamaIndex if the core problem is RAG pipeline quality itself (chunking, indexing, retrieval); LangChain for general-purpose orchestration gluing together many different tool types; LangGraph or CrewAI when the design is genuinely multi-agent with distinct roles that need to converse or loop, and you want explicit, inspectable control over a cyclic execution graph; and for a single-agent, single-source system, consider skipping a framework entirely — a hand-rolled loop against the raw model API has less overhead and is easier to debug than an unnecessary abstraction layer.

questions.title: Walk through a concrete example of why single-shot RAG fails on a genuinely compound question, and how an agentic version fixes it.
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Take "my basement flooded from a burst pipe and my car got water damage, am I covered?" — single-shot RAG embeds the whole compound question once and runs one search, which creates three distinct failure points: if auto and homeowner's policies live in the same index, whichever has denser chunks near that embedding dominates the top-k and the other policy's relevant clause may not make the cut at all; even if both surface, nothing checks that the retrieved "water damage" clause actually addresses *flood* specifically (homeowner's policies typically exclude flood while covering other water damage — a distinction a single pass has no mechanism to check); and there's no re-query if the first pull is thin. An agentic version decomposes into policy-specific subqueries, retrieves each independently, and runs an explicit verification step checking for exactly this kind of nuance before synthesizing a final answer.

questions.title: Which query needs a knowledge graph rather than a vector index?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A vector index retrieves by embedding similarity, which is excellent for open-ended semantic queries but has no mechanism for following explicit entity relationships across documents — it can't natively answer "who leads the company that acquired the company that made this product." A knowledge graph stores entities and typed relationships explicitly, enabling that kind of multi-hop structured traversal directly, but it's a worse fit for free-form "find me things that feel similar to this" queries a graph has no edges to represent. Production systems commonly run both: vector search to find semantic entry points into the graph, graph traversal for the relational reasoning once you're in.

questions.title: How do you handle entity resolution when the same real-world entity shows up under different names across documents?

questions.answer: A tiered approach, cheapest first: normalize surface forms (lowercase, strip punctuation, expand known abbreviations); apply a curated alias table for known synonyms (ticker symbols, legal name variants); use embedding similarity to cluster candidate names above a cosine threshold (roughly 0.92 is a common starting point); and for genuinely ambiguous remaining cases, prompt an LLM with surrounding context to make the call. Assign each resolved cluster a single canonical node ID and store every surface form as an alias on it, so future documents referencing any variant resolve to the same node.

questions.title: Why does source provenance on every graph edge matter operationally, not just for citation purposes?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Without knowing which source document produced a given edge, you can't incrementally update the graph when that document changes or gets deleted — you'd have no way to know which edges to remove, and would be forced to rebuild the entire graph from scratch on every single document change. With provenance tracked per edge, a document update becomes a targeted operation: delete that document's edges, re-extract from the new version, done — the difference between an incremental update pipeline and a full rebuild every time anything changes.

questions.title: Which question needs GraphRAG's global search rather than local search?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Local search behaves like standard knowledge-graph RAG: vector similarity finds entry-point entities, then it expands into their graph neighborhood to assemble context for one generation call — cheap and precise for entity-anchored questions. Global search instead map-reduces over pre-generated community summaries (computed once at index time via Leiden clustering): each relevant community summary independently produces a partial answer, and those partial answers get ranked and merged into one final response — costs more per query, but it's the only mode that can actually answer broad, thematic, corpus-wide questions, since the expensive summarization work was already paid for once upfront rather than repeated per query.

questions.title: When do you choose a knowledge graph over pure vector retrieval, as a real design decision?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.

questions.answer: When queries genuinely require multi-hop reasoning across named entities, when you need to retrieve by relationship type rather than general topical similarity ("find all companies Apple acquired"), when entity deduplication materially affects answer quality because multiple documents refer to the same thing inconsistently, or when the domain already has a well-defined ontology (medical codes, legal concepts, product hierarchies) a graph can map onto directly. Stick with vector retrieval when queries are primarily free-form/semantic, the corpus lacks any clear entity structure to exploit, or build time is genuinely constrained — a graph you don't have time to build and maintain correctly is worse than no graph at all.

questions.title: What's the “sliding window” memory problem, and how does compress-and-carry solve it?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A sliding window keeps only the last N turns verbatim — once it fills, older turns are simply dropped, and the system loses all memory of earlier conversation context, even context that might matter several turns later. Compress-and-carry periodically compresses older turns into a short running summary and carries that summary forward instead of the raw turns, so the context cost grows with summary length rather than linearly with session length — the tradeoff is the summary loses precision (exact quotes, fine phrasing nuance), which is why it's usually paired with a sliding window over the *most recent* few turns kept verbatim for immediate fidelity.

questions.title: How does MemGPT's approach to memory differ from a standard application-managed sliding window or summary?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Standard approaches manage memory entirely outside the model — the application layer decides what to keep, archive, or drop. MemGPT instead gives the model explicit memory-management tools (append to working memory, search archival memory, insert into archival memory) and lets the model itself decide when to invoke them, the same way it decides when to call a retrieval tool. The upside is the model can reason about *what's actually worth remembering* in a way a fixed window or summary rule can't ("this constraint will matter several turns from now"); the downside is added latency from the memory tool calls themselves, and the risk of the model mismanaging memory if those tool prompts aren't specified carefully.

questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.

questions.answer: After each session ends, run a lightweight extraction pass asking "what did we learn about this user's preferences, constraints, or domain knowledge this session," and store only those extracted facts in a per-user namespaced vector store — not the raw transcript. At the start of a new session, retrieve the most relevant stored facts for the opening query and inject them as a brief "user context" block in the system prompt. Storing semantic summaries rather than full transcripts is both cheaper and aligned with minimal-data-retention practice — you rarely actually need the verbatim history, just the durable facts it revealed.

questions.title: How does CLIP's training objective enable cross-modal retrieval without any manually labeled image-text pairs?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: It trains contrastively on hundreds of millions of naturally co-occurring (image, alt-text) pairs scraped from the web — no manual labeling involved — with a loss that pulls each image's embedding close to its paired text embedding and pushes it away from the other images in the same training batch. Because both encoders are trained to land in the same shared vector space, a text query can be embedded and compared directly against image embeddings by ordinary cosine similarity at retrieval time, with no classification head or extra alignment step needed.

questions.title: Early fusion vs. late fusion for multimodal RAG — which do production systems actually use, and why?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Early fusion combines raw multimodal inputs before encoding, requiring one architecture capable of processing both modalities jointly from the start. Late fusion encodes each modality independently with its own best-in-class encoder (text with a strong text embedder, images with CLIP) and combines the resulting vectors afterward — and this is what production systems overwhelmingly use, because it lets you swap in the best available encoder per modality without retraining anything else, index everything in one shared vector store with a single ANN query across modalities, and add a brand-new modality later (audio, say) by adding one new encoder rather than retraining the whole system.

questions.title: How would you index a corpus of PDFs that mix prose, figures, and tables?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Parse each document and route by content type: text blocks chunked and embedded with a text encoder; figures extracted as images and embedded with CLIP (or captioned via a vision-language model and embedded as text, for cases where a text query is more likely than an image query); tables linearized to Markdown and embedded as text. Store everything in one index with a `modality` metadata field so retrieval can span all three at once from a single text query embedding — and flag any figure that has no surrounding caption text for manual review, since those are the hardest content type for a plain text query to ever surface via semantic similarity alone.

questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.

questions.title: Beyond RAGAS, what other LLM-judge evaluation frameworks exist, and when would you reach for each?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: ARES adds calibrated confidence intervals to judge scores at the cost of needing domain fine-tuning and a few hundred human labels — worth it when you need statistically defensible scores, not just a point estimate. RAGChecker gives claim-level diagnostics that separate retriever failure from generator failure, useful specifically when RAGAS or production has already flagged *that* something's wrong but not *which stage*. ConsJudge trains a judge model from judgment-consistency signals rather than human labels or a stronger reference model, useful if you want your own judge without depending on either. FaithJudge is a human-aligned hallucination-rate leaderboard, useful for picking a generator (or judge) model with an independent, pre-validated hallucination-rate comparison rather than trusting a vendor's own benchmark.

questions.title: How do you measure citation quality in a verifiable RAG system, beyond “does it have citations at all”?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Three genuinely separate metrics, because they catch three different failure modes: citation precision (of the passages actually cited, what fraction genuinely support the claim next to them — measured via NLI entailment between the cited passage and the specific claim); citation recall (of the claims the response makes, what fraction have any citation at all — requires segmenting the response into atomic claims first); and attribution accuracy (does the cited passage actually say what the response claims it says, which is distinct from hallucination detection, since hallucination checks if *any* passage supports a claim, while attribution accuracy checks specifically whether *the cited one* does).

questions.title: How do you evaluate RAG answers for open-ended questions where there's no single correct reference answer?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Automated exact-match metrics are useless here, so lean on two complementary LLM-judge patterns instead: rubric-based absolute scoring (define explicit dimensions — relevance, completeness, accuracy, citation quality — and have a strong judge model score each independently, which forces reproducibility and makes variance explainable) and pairwise preference (show the judge two responses — a baseline and a candidate — and ask which is better overall; pairwise judgments are empirically more reliable than absolute scores because they anchor the judge to a concrete comparison rather than an abstract scale). Always calibrate whichever you use against a small set of human-labeled examples before trusting it at scale.

questions.title: How do you evaluate a RAG system when you have no ground-truth labels at all?

questions.answer: "You can't" is the wrong answer here. Reference-free LLM-as-judge techniques genuinely work for faithfulness specifically, because checking whether an answer's claims are supported by the retrieved context only needs the context and the answer — it never needed a gold reference answer in the first place. Combine that with behavioral signals from live traffic (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, escalation rate) to triangulate overall quality without any labeled data at all.

questions.title: Your offline eval scores improved after a change, but users are complaining more. What's going on?

Check the unanswerable-question rate and compare query distributions between the golden set and live traffic before concluding anything about the model itself regressed.

questions.title: Your LLM-judge scores dropped 5% overnight with no deploy on your side. What do you check first?

questions.answer: Don't assume your system broke — the drop could be coming from the *judge* itself. Providers silently update underlying judge models, and that alone can shift every score without any genuine change in your system's output quality. The fix is scoring a fixed sentinel set daily (same inputs, same expected scores, run every day regardless of anything else) — a shift in the sentinel set's scores isolates judge drift from a genuine system regression immediately, instead of you spending hours investigating a system problem that doesn't exist.

questions.title: How would you know your RAG system's quality regressed after a deploy, in a real production setup?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Four layers, and naming all four (in order) is what separates a senior answer from "we have an eval set": a pre-deploy CI gate running the golden-dataset eval that blocks the deploy on any metric regression beyond threshold; a canary rollout to a small traffic slice, comparing guardrail metrics (latency, error rate, refusal rate) and judge scores canary-vs-control before full rollout; post-rollout online signals (regeneration rate, rephrase rate, thumbs ratio, escalation rate) watched against a pre-deploy baseline window; and trace-level triage when any signal fires — pulling the actual failing traces, localizing which stage broke using per-stage scores, and promoting those failures into the golden set so the exact same regression gets caught pre-deploy the next time around.

questions.title: Where does the money actually go in a RAG system's per-query cost, and which stage dominates?

questions.title: Each request has a 6,000-token fixed prefix and 500 tokens that vary. Cached input tokens cost 10% of the normal price. If every request hits the cache, by what percentage does the input cost fall?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer:
The 6,000 cached tokens now cost 10% of normal, a saving of 90% on 6,000 of the 6,500 input tokens: 6,000 × 0.9 ÷ 6,500 = **83.1%**. That only holds if the prefix stays byte-identical and requests arrive within the cache's lifetime.

The provider caches the computed KV attention tensors for the static part of your prompt (a system prompt, a stable reference-document prefix) and charges a small fraction of the full input-token price on a cache hit instead of full price — the dollar amounts shift with pricing updates, but the ratio (a fraction of full price on a hit) is the stable fact worth remembering. It only pays off if your prompt prefix stays byte-identical across requests — even a whitespace difference busts the cache — and if there's enough request volume hitting that same prefix within the cache's TTL window (typically minutes) to actually benefit from it; a system with highly unique, rarely-repeated prompts gets little from this lever.

questions.title: What is model tiering in a RAG pipeline, and when is it actually safe to downgrade to a cheaper model for a given stage?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Assigning each pipeline stage to the cheapest model that clears that stage's specific quality bar, rather than running the same large model everywhere — routing/classification, simple query rewrites, and binary relevance checks are all usually safe to downgrade to a small, fast model, while multi-document synthesis, complex reasoning chains, and ambiguous or nuance-sensitive generation stay on the larger model. The discipline that makes this safe: measure the quality regression empirically per stage rather than assuming a stage is "simple enough" — a stage that looks trivial can still have a real quality cliff on a cheaper model if you never checked.

questions.title: Walk through how you'd actually reduce a RAG system's monthly LLM spend from, say, $10K to something meaningfully lower.
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: In rough ROI order: enable prompt caching on the static system prompt and any stable reference material first — this alone commonly cuts 70–95% of the cost on cached prefixes; set tight, type-specific `max_tokens` budgets rather than one generous default for every query; add a cheap classifier to route simple factual queries to a smaller model instead of your default large one; add a semantic query cache for genuinely high-frequency repeated questions; and consider compressing retrieved chunks with a small model before handing them to the large generation model. These five, stacked, typically cut cost 60–80% with limited quality impact — but each should be measured against your golden set individually, not assumed to be safe.

questions.title: What's the difference between exact-match caching, semantic caching, and provider-side prompt caching in a RAG system?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: Exact-match caching keys on the verbatim query string — only byte-identical repeats hit. Semantic caching embeds the incoming query and checks similarity against previously-served queries, so differently-phrased-but-equivalent questions can share a cached response, at the real cost of false-positive risk (similar embeddings, genuinely different intent). Provider-side prompt caching is a different thing entirely — it's server-side KV-tensor caching for a static prompt prefix, still runs real inference just more cheaply, versus the other two which skip inference entirely on a hit and return a stored response.

questions.title: What's a cache stampede, and how do you prevent one in a RAG caching layer?
questions.context: Answer in your own words, then compare with the worked explanation.
criteria: Answer the question directly and accurately.
Explain the mechanism or calculation behind your answer.
Address the assumptions and trade-offs that matter here.
questions.answer: A popular cache entry expires (or the cache is cold after a restart), and many concurrent requests for that same key all miss simultaneously, each independently re-running the expensive underlying operation — generation, re-embedding, retrieval — wasting compute and potentially overwhelming the backend all at once. Standard preventions: request coalescing/single-flight (only the first miss actually recomputes; concurrent requests for the same key wait on that result instead of duplicating the work), a lock around the recompute-and-write step so only one caller repopulates the entry, probabilistic early expiration (recompute slightly before the real TTL, with increasing probability as expiry nears, to spread refreshes out instead of letting them all cliff-edge together), and proactive cache warming ahead of a known traffic spike or right after a deploy/restart.
